summary: An island nation in the South Pacific made up of nine atolls and coral islands, one of the least populous countries in the world; its extremely low elevation leaves it deeply threatened by sea-level rise. It became independent in 1978.

ranking.name: Church of Tuvalu
ranking.description: In 1861, Elekana, a deacon from the Cook Islands, was blown off course in his canoe and drifted to Nukulaelae, where he began preaching to the islanders. The London Missionary Society then stationed Samoan pastors on the islands, and Christianity rapidly replaced the traditional beliefs. This Congregationalist church developed into the Church of Tuvalu around the time of independence in 1978; village life on every island revolves around the church, which is why it is by far the dominant religion.

ranking.name: Other Christian denominations (Seventh-day Adventists, Brethren, Catholics, etc.)
ranking.description: Denominations such as the Seventh-day Adventists, the Brethren and the Catholic Church arrived successively during the 20th century, and some Tuvaluans who worked or studied abroad also brought new denominations home. Because the Church of Tuvalu holds a secure place in island society and in the traditional councils, these groups are all very small and are concentrated mainly in the capital, Funafuti.

ranking.name: Bahá'í Faith
ranking.description: The Bahá'í Faith reached Tuvalu in the mid-20th century and formed a relatively concentrated community on Nanumea in the north. Emphasizing the oneness of humanity and education, it has set up community activities on the islands, but its followers still make up only a very small share of the population.

ranking.name: Others (Islam, etc.)
ranking.description: Other faiths include small groups such as the Ahmadiyya branch of Islam, which arrived in recent decades. In a country where the Church of Tuvalu is the core of society, the spread of new religions often raises concern among traditional village leaders, so the number of adherents is very small.

religion.background: The Tuvaluans originally worshipped ancestors and nature spirits, and each island had its own gods and taboos. From 1861, missionaries from the Cook Islands and Samoa, supported by the London Missionary Society, began preaching; Christianity spread rapidly, and Samoan pastors led the church for a long time. Tuvalu became a British protectorate in 1892, was later joined with the Gilbert Islands as a colony, and became independent in 1978. Today the Church of Tuvalu is the center of society and culture, while other denominations and religions account for only small minorities.

language.official: The official languages are Tuvaluan and English.

ranking.name: Tuvaluan
ranking.description: Tuvaluan belongs to the Polynesian branch of languages and descends from the speech of settlers who migrated from Samoa, Tonga and elsewhere several hundred years ago; the islands are divided into northern and southern dialects. During the colonial period, the church and schools long used Samoan, but Tuvaluan always remained the everyday language of homes and villages. After independence in 1978 it became a symbol of national identity, and the great majority of citizens speak it as their mother tongue.

ranking.name: Kiribati (Gilbertese)
ranking.description: Speakers of Gilbertese are concentrated on Nui, whose inhabitants historically were influenced by the arrival of Micronesians from the Gilbert Islands and still use Gilbertese as their main language. From 1916 to 1975, Tuvalu (the Ellice Islands) and the Gilbert Islands belonged to the same British colony, and many Tuvaluans worked or were educated in Kiribati, which also gave Gilbertese some influence in Tuvalu.

ranking.name: English
ranking.description: English was introduced as the language of administration and education during British colonial rule. Today, together with Tuvaluan, it is an official language, used in government documents, law, secondary education and international affairs. Because the population is tiny and must communicate with the outside world, English is very important, but very few people speak it as a mother tongue.

language.history: Tuvaluan belongs to the Polynesian branch and is closely related to Samoan and Tokelauan; only on Nui is Gilbertese, a Micronesian language, spoken. In the late 19th century, Samoan pastors preached and ran schools on the islands, making Samoan the language of the church and education for a long time. English became the official language during the British colonial period. After the separation from the Gilbert Islands in 1975 and independence in 1978, Tuvaluan came to be regarded as the core of national identity and began to be promoted in school education.

ranking.name: Pulaka (swamp taro)
ranking.description: A large swamp taro grown for several years in deep pits dug into the coral island before it can be harvested; once cooked it has a smooth, creamy texture and is often prepared with coconut milk.
ranking.history: Because atoll soil is poor, the ancestors of the Tuvaluans dug deep pits in the coral islands down to the freshwater lens and then filled them layer by layer with decayed leaves as compost to grow pulaka, a farming method that has lasted for hundreds of years. Pulaka takes a long time to grow and is labor-intensive to cultivate, so it holds a lofty place at weddings and festivals, and large taro corms symbolize a family's diligence and wealth. In recent years, rising seas have seeped seawater into the taro pits and reduced pulaka yields, making it a conspicuous example of how climate change affects Tuvalu.

ranking.name: Coconut crab
ranking.description: The coconut crab is the largest land-dwelling arthropod; steamed or roasted, its meat is sweet and carries a coconut aroma, and it is often eaten at festive banquets.
ranking.history: The coconut crab is famous for being able to husk coconuts with its powerful claws, and its long diet of coconuts gives its meat a distinctive coconut flavor. On resource-limited atolls, it has traditionally been an important source of protein and a prized ingredient for entertaining honored guests and for festive feasts. Because of overharvesting, coconut crab numbers have declined on many Pacific islands, and some Tuvaluan islands have also introduced harvest management.

ranking.name: Breadfruit
ranking.description: Breadfruit is a large starchy fruit that can be roasted, boiled or fried, or fermented and buried underground for long-term storage; it is often cooked with coconut milk.
ranking.history: Breadfruit is one of the crops that the Austronesian ancestors carried by canoe to the Pacific islands, and on atolls it is one of the few starchy foods that can be produced in quantity. Traditionally, islanders ferment breadfruit and bury it in underground pits to preserve it against food shortages caused by typhoons or drought. Although imported rice and flour are increasingly common today, breadfruit remains a traditional staple at family meals and festive banquets.

ranking.name: Pandanus fruit
ranking.description: The pandanus fruit is made up of many wedge-shaped segments; one can chew them directly to suck out the sweet juice of the flesh, or cook and mash them into a paste or dry them into dried fruit.
ranking.history: Pandanus is salt-tolerant and drought-tolerant, one of the very few fruit trees on an atoll able to grow in poor coral sand, and it has traditionally been an important source of food and vitamins for the Tuvaluans. The dried fruit keeps for a long time, suiting sea voyages and lean years, while the leaves are woven into mats, baskets and roofing. Pandanus is therefore inseparable from Tuvaluan diet, crafts and island life.

ranking.name: Coconut sap (toddy)
ranking.description: Sweet sap collected by cutting the flower bud of the coconut palm; it can be drunk fresh, boiled down into syrup or fermented into an alcoholic drink, and has a light, sweet coconut flavor.
ranking.history: On atolls that lack sugarcane and other sources of sweetness, collecting coconut sap is a traditional Tuvaluan skill, and men climb coconut palms every morning and evening to cut the flower buds and collect the sap. Coconut sap is nutritious and was often given to children in the past, while the syrup boiled down from it keeps for a long time and is used in cooking. The fermented toddy is drunk on social occasions, and the craft is still passed down on the islands today.
